One of the important yet under-examined questions in Iran's contemporary history is why Iran, in the age of colonialism, despite its economic and military weakness and its proximity to two great imperial powers, managed to preserve its political independence and avoid becoming a formal colony. In the nineteenth century, before the discovery of oil, Iran—unlike India—did not possess vast, contiguous agricultural lands with a high capacity for producing commercial crops. Unlike China, it had no consumer market with a population in the hundreds of millions, and unlike certain other territories, known gold and silver mines were not the primary source of its economic appeal to colonial powers. Nor was Iran part of the Ottoman Empire, such that it would have been caught up in the partition of Ottoman territories among the European powers. Nevertheless, Iran held extraordinary geopolitical importance. Its geographic position—between Tsarist Russia and British-ruled India—had made the country one of the most important arenas of imperial rivalry. Under such circumstances, Iran's survival cannot be attributed merely to chance or to a lack of resources attractive to colonialists. A man of building ▪️ Mohsen Khalili Iraqi passed away today, 17 Mehr 1405. A man whose name was intertwined with industry, entrepreneurship, and resilience. His passing marks the loss of one of the enduring figures of Iran's industry. An industrialist whose life demonstrated that building a factory is only the beginning of the journey, and that the greater art lies in keeping it alive through difficult times and passing it on to future generations. ▪️ Khalili Iraqi, born in 1308, grew up in a family where work and initiative held a special place. His father, Mahmoud Khalili, was one of the pioneers of Iran's industry, and Mohsen set out alongside him on a path that led to the founding of Butan. Father and son saw an opportunity to improve people's lives in the gases that flared above the oil wells. The fruit of this vision was the expansion of liquid gas use and subsequently the production of gas appliances, which wove industry into the daily lives of Iranian families. ▪️ He belonged to a generation that saw industry as a path to the nation's prosperity. Involvement in industrial associations and efforts to strengthen cooperation among producers formed another part of his legacy. In this vision, the progress of one factory was inseparable from the fate of other enterprises, and defending production required cooperation and organization among industrialists. His professional life, of course, was not without hardship. After the revolution, part of Butan's shares were subject to confiscation orders, and the Khalili family struggled for years to reclaim them. From what I have heard, Mohsen Khalili appeared in court 254 times to win back his company. He and his partners, in order to keep the company afloat and pay the workers' wages, even sold their personal properties. This act of standing firm is one of the brightest chapters of his life. ▪️ In his final years, the concern for development never left his mind. He dedicated part of his wealth to industrial research, and through the establishment of the Mohsen Khalili Iraqi Industrial Development Foundation, he supported the study of the challenges of Iran's industrialization. Supporting economists' research was a continuation of the very path he had begun decades earlier in the workshop and the factory. An effort to find ways to build a more prosperous Iran. From the bottom of my heart, I offer my condolences to the honorable family and friends of Engineer Khalili on his passing. May his soul rest in peace and his memory be cherished ☑️ Mohsen Jalalpour mohsenjalalpour
